TITLE: Hybrid Generative-Regression Model for Brain Encoding
PROPOSAL: Design a hybrid model that leverages the strengths of regression-based and generative strategies for brain encoding. Specifically, employ a deterministic neural decoder with variational autoencoder (VAE) architecture to learn the distribution of neural responses to visual stimuli. Then, use this learned prior to condition a probabilistic fMRI synthesizer, enabling the generation of voxel-level fMRI responses that capture both the variability and functional consistency of neural activity.
CONTROLS: 
- Baseline regression model (e.g., linear regression, neural network regression) to predict fMRI responses from visual stimuli.
- Ablation of the VAE architecture, using a deterministic VAE for the prior.
- Baseline generative model (e.g., MindSimulator) with random initialization without prior knowledge of the prior distribution of neural responses.
COST: 100 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: The hybrid approach significantly improves the consistency and realism of generated fMRI responses, especially when compared to a standard regression-based model and a stochastic generative model without prior knowledge of the prior distribution of neural responses; However, this improvement comes at a higher computational cost, making the approach less scalable for very large datasets. 

Additionally, evaluate its performance in fMRI-to-image decoding tasks by functioning as a more tractable training data augmentation approach compared to real fMRI data.

PROPOSAL: Adapt the hybrid model to incorporate temporal variability in fMRI synthesis. Specifically, use a recurrent neural network (RNN) architecture to capture time series patterns in brain activity and augment the probabilistic fMRI synthesizer with a farthest point sampling (FPS) strategy to introduce variability while maintaining functional consistency across trials.
CONTROLS: 
- Baseline hybrid model without RNN or FPS for temporal variability.
- Ablation of FPS strategy, using a standard sampling approach without FPS.
- Using a pre-trained RNN on high-level visual features rather than raw fMRI data for conditioning.
COST: 200 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: The inclusion of RNN and FPS significantly improves the ability of the hybrid model to capture trial-to-trial variability in fMRI responses, while still maintaining the functional consistency of the responses over time; However, the improvement comes at the cost of increased computational complexity and potential mode collapse due to the FPS strategy.

Evaluate the extent to which this adapted model can capture temporal variability in fMRI responses across trials and also assess its performance in fMRI-to-image decoding tasks.

TITLE: Subject-Specific Brain Encoding: Unsupervised Domain Adaptation
PROPOSAL: Design an unsupervised domain adaptation approach to adapt the brain encoding model from a source domain (e.g., a large dataset of fMRI recordings) to a target domain (e.g., a new subject with limited or no available fMRI data). This approach will enable the model to generalize better across subjects and learn subject-specific brain encoding patterns.
CONTROLS: 
- Baseline model trained on a single subject or dataset.
- Ablation of domain-invariant features, using a standard brain encoding model without adaptation.
- Baseline model with domain adaptation, but without unsupervised domain adaptation.
COST: 150 GPU-hours

Expect the proposed approach to improve the model's ability to generalize across subjects, enabling better cross-subject transfer learning and reducing the need for large amounts of labeled data, making it more applicable in real-world scenarios. Potential challenges might arise from the increased complexity of the adaptation process and the risk of overfitting to the source domain.

TITLE: Multi-Task Learning for Brain Encoding and Decoding
PROPOSAL: Implement a multi-task learning approach by training the brain encoding model jointly with an fMRI-to-image decoding model. This will enable the model to learn shared representations that are beneficial for both tasks, ultimately improving its ability to generate realistic fMRI responses and accurately reconstruct visual stimuli from brain activity.
CONTROLS: 
- Baseline models (brain encoding and fMRI-to-image decoding) trained separately.
- Ablation of shared representations, using standard separate models.
- Baseline multi-task learning, but without shared representations.
COST: 300 GPU-hours

Expect the proposed multi-task learning approach to improve the model's ability to capture high-level visual features and spatial patterns in brain activity, making it more accurate and effective in both brain encoding and fMRI-to-image decoding tasks. Potential challenges might arise from the increased complexity of the multi-task learning process and the risk of overfitting to the joint training objectives.

TITLE: Exploring the Impact of Spatial and Temporal Downsampling on Brain Encoding
PROPOSAL: Investigate the effects of spatial and temporal downsampling on the accuracy and robustness of brain encoding models. This includes evaluating the impact of different sampling rates on fMRI data and the model's ability to generalize to different spatial and temporal resolutions.
CONTROLS: 
- Baseline model trained on full-resolution fMRI data.

Expect the proposed study to provide insights into the limits of brain encoding models with respect to spatial and temporal resolution and to improve their ability to generalize to real-world scenarios with varying data quality and resolution. Potential challenges might arise from the increased complexity of the analysis and the need for larger training datasets to account for the effects of downsampling.

TITLE: Non-Deterministic Brain Encoding via Latent Diffusions
PROPOSAL: We propose a non-deterministic brain encoding model based on latent diffusion processes to capture the one-to-many variations in neural responses. Specifically, we use a neural network to transform visual inputs into a latent space, followed by a learned diffusion process that captures the variability of neural responses. This process is conditioned on the visual stimulus and utilizes a stochastic hierarchical latent variable model to generate diverse yet functionally consistent neural patterns. At inference time, we use a sampling-based method, such as Langevin dynamics or Hamiltonian Monte Carlo, to draw samples from the learned diffusion process.
CONTROLS: We will compare our approach to the MindSimulator with diffusion sampling, as well as linear regression, Ridge regression, and a vanilla autoregressive model conditioning on visual stimuli.
COST: Estimated 1000 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: We expect to see improved performance in terms of generating diverse neural patterns that encode the same visual stimulus, and also reducing the gap between synthetic and real fMRI responses. However, we may face challenges in modeling the strength of one-to-many variability, leading to unrealistic or inconsistent patterns.

TITLE: Evaluating Cross-Subject Transferability of Brain Encoding Models
PROPOSAL: We conduct experiments to evaluate the cross-subject transferability of our non-deterministic brain encoding model, comparing it to existing deterministic methods, such as linear regression and MindSimulator. Specifically, we train each model on fMRI data from a subset of subjects and evaluate their performance on unseen subjects from distinct cohorts. We also investigate the properties of the learned latent spaces to understand how they relate to individual differences in brain structure and function.
CONTROLS: We will use datasets from multiple sources, such as OpenfMRI and lavalablack fMRI datasets, and split them into training and testing sets. We will also compare our results to a baseline of training models on each subject individually.
COST: Estimated 2500 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: We expect to see improved cross-subject transferability of our non-deterministic brain encoding model, as it learns to capture generalizable representations of neural encoding across subjects. However, we may encounter challenges in generalizing to entirely new subjects with different scanning protocols, age groups, or cohorts, which may limit the applicability of our models in real-world settings.
